papers.version_note: Single web page (QCi Resource library lesson), no page breaks in the text layer; copyright line reads 2018-2026.
papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc educational lesson that defines unconventional computing and describes probabilistic, analog and continuous-time computing in relation to the vendor's EQC and reservoir products.

assertions.value: The authors define unconventional computing as any type of computing done in a way that is not the usual way, and state that they keep the definition informal.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Computing in new and creative ways
quotes: Unconventional computing is any type of computing done in a way that is not the usual way
it makes sense to keep the way unconventional is defined somewhat informal
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states this as its own definition.

assertions.value: The authors state that a few processors working together, or a computer that uses trinary variables instead of binary variables, would not be very unconventional for their purposes.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Computing in new and creative ways
quotes: having a few processors that work together isn't that unconventional
wouldn't be very unconventional. The basic concept is the same, just a detail is different.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states this as its own definition.

assertions.value: The authors state that the lesson does not cover the entire field of unconventional computing and focuses on the parts relevant to QCi products that may be practically useful.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Computing in new and creative ways
quotes: this lesson will not cover the entire field of unconventional computing
We will rather focus on those which are relevant to our products, and which may be practically useful.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states this as its own scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that the practical case for unconventional computing is that some tasks exist where the conventional approach struggles, and that for most tasks conventional computers work just fine.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Why unconventional?
quotes: An answer here is that for most tasks conventional computers work just fine.
The practical case for unconventional computing is that there are some tasks where the conventional approach struggles
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: The authors present the graphics card as a historical example: image parts are calculated in parallel on a chip with many processors, each with a small amount of memory. They add that it is debatable whether GPU computing is still unconventional.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Why unconventional?
quotes: The solution is to calculate different parts of the image in parallel with a chip that has many processors, each with a small amount of memory.
it is probably debatable whether GPU computing can really still be considered "unconventional"
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: QCi states that its unconventional computers address tasks where conventional techniques struggle: hard optimization problems with the EQC (entropy quantum computing) paradigm, and machine learning with minimum training in the reservoir paradigm.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Why unconventional?
quotes: QCi's unconventional computers address different tasks where the more conventional techniques struggle.
These include solving hard optimization problems, with the EQC (entropy quantum computing) paradigm and performing machine learning with minimum training in the reservoir paradigm
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own products; the page gives no benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors state that requiring a computer to be universal is too limiting, because an unconventional computer that solves one important problem could be useful without being universal. They give analog tide predicting machines as a historical example.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section What is computing?
quotes: Another option would be to require a computer to be universal, capable in principle of performing any computation given enough time.
an unconventional computer that is good at solving one particularly important problem could be useful without being universal
analog tide predicting machines
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that, according to researchers on the topic, computation relies on an abstract model of what the system does, where information is programmed into the system and read out, with the physical system acting as a stand-in for the model.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section What is computing?
quotes: The answer, according to researchers on the topic, is that computation relies on having an abstract model of what the system is doing
information is programmed into the system and eventually read out, with the physical system acting as a stand-in for the model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page attributes the idea to unnamed researchers and names no reference in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in this idea of computing, almost anything can be a computer if it is used as one, but just existing does not make a system a computer.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section What is computing?
quotes: almost anything can be a computer if it is used as one but just existing doesn't make a system a computer
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: QCi states that it offers a reservoir computer as a product, that the product uses a photonic system, and that the system is somewhat more complex than a bucket of water. The authors note that some of the earliest ideas of reservoir computers considered the reservoir to be a literal bucket of water.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section What is computing?
quotes: some of the earliest ideas of reservoir computers considered the reservoir to be a literal bucket of water
We offer a reservoir computer as one of our products, but it uses a photonic system that is somewhat more complex than a bucket of water
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that conventional computers are deterministic: a set determined series of events happens for a given input, and any deviation is an error that is exceedingly rare in a properly functioning conventional computer.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Probabilistic Computers
quotes: Conventional computers, like the one you are probably using to read this article, are deterministic.
any deviation from this behavior is an error
errors do happen but they are exceedingly rare in a properly functioning conventional computer
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: The authors define a probabilistic computer as one whose actions are well-defined but with an element of randomness in how it behaves. They avoid the term non-deterministic because it has a particular meaning in complexity theory.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Probabilistic Computers
quotes: An alternative is to design a computer where the actions of the computer are well-defined, but there is an element of randomness in how the computer behaves.
We will call this a probabilistic computer, while intentionally avoiding the term "non-deterministic"
since that has a particular meaning in complexity theory
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines its own term in the section Probabilistic Computers.

assertions.value: The authors state that the most conventional way to do probabilistic computation is a deterministic computer that takes randomly generated numbers as inputs, and that one QCi product is a random number generator that does this.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Probabilistic Computers
quotes: The most "conventional" way to perform probabilistic computation is to use a deterministic computer but use some randomly generated numbers as inputs to make some choices randomly.
One of our products is a device that does exactly this , a random number generator.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since quantum mechanical processes are fundamentally probabilistic because of how quantum measurement works, the QCi EQC paradigm is one example of fundamentally probabilistic computing where the randomness is built into the computer itself.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Probabilistic Computers
quotes: A more unconventional application of probabilistic computing is to use a computer where the inherent randomness is actually built into the computer itself.
Since quantum mechanical processes are fundamentally probabilistic (thanks to how quantum measurement works), our EQC paradigm is one example of fundamentally probabilistic computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own paradigm; the page gives no derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that conventional computers are digital and define ones and zeros as voltages within certain ranges separated by a range of voltages considered forbidden. A voltage passes through the forbidden values quickly when it switches, so the model can treat the change as instantaneous.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: conventional computers define ones and zeros as voltages being within certain ranges that are separated by a range of voltages that are considered "forbidden"
even a digital computer would have to have a voltage pass through the forbidden values, but this happens quickly
Therefore this model can be discrete and treat the change as instantaneous.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that a classical computer whose allowed states are continuous would be an analog computer, with values that change continuously over time.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: A classical computer where the allowed states are continuous would be an analog computer that can have values that change continuously over time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines an analog computer in the section Analog and Continuous-time Computers.

assertions.value: The authors state that gate-model quantum computing is the closest analogy to digital computing in a quantum setting, since it defines discrete quantum operations (gates) similarly to the operations of conventional digital computers.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: The closest analogy to digital computing in a quantum setting is gate-model quantum computing, where discrete quantum operations (gates) are defined similarly to the operations performed in conventional digital computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: QCi states that its core technology could be used to build gate-model computers, that more unconventional models can be less demanding in noise levels and in technology, and that these models are its current focus.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: While our core technology could be used to build gate-model computers
More unconventional models can be less demanding in terms of noise levels and less demanding for the technology, so they are our current focus.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own technology and focus; the page gives no noise figures.
assertions.reader_inference: The page states no noise threshold and gives no comparison, so the claim is qualitative.

assertions.value: The authors state that computing on a discrete state space in a way that is continuous in time is a uniquely quantum proposition, because a quantum superposition can change continuously over time while a classical bit either flips or does not.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: Computing on a discrete state space, but in a way that is continuous in time is a uniquely quantum proposition.
Classically, if a bit is in the state 1 1 1 , then it either flips to state 0 0 0 or it doesn't
Quantum mechanically, however, it is possible to continuously change a superposition over time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: The authors give an example of a single-qubit state whose two amplitudes change continuously in time, with normalization required at all times, from the first basis state at the start to the second basis state at the end. They say this effectively flips a bit over time.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: note that normalization requires
effectively flipping a bit over time
then I can imagine that I can change a and b continuously
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The example is a thought experiment; the page does not name a physical system that realizes it.

assertions.value: The authors state that a measurement at any time finds outcome zero with probability given by the squared magnitude of the first amplitude and outcome one with probability given by the squared magnitude of the second amplitude, with no chance of any other outcome.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: I can measure at any time and I will always find a 0 0 0 outcome with probability ∣ a ( t ) ∣ 2
and a 1 1 1 outcome with probability ∣ b ( t ) ∣ 2
and there is no chance of any other outcome
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that a continuously changing superposition is fundamentally different from a classical probability distribution that changes continuously overall, and that where an underlying system still undergoes discrete jumps, hidden variable models are not possible in general for quantum systems.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: This is fundamentally different from a classical probability distribution, which may change continuously overall.
such hidden variable models are not possible in general for quantum systems
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The page cites no theorem here; the statement is plausibly a reference to Bell-type results, but the page does not say so.

assertions.value: The authors state that in a continuous-time quantum walk, Hamiltonian elements that flip bit values and terms that describe an optimization problem are active at the same time. They describe the system as digital in one sense, because it has two discrete outcomes, and analog in another, because the operation is continuous and the state is well-defined at all points.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: The simplest example is a continuous-time quantum walk , where Hamiltonian elements that flip bit values as well as terms that describe an optimization problem are active at the same time.
In one sense such a system is digital because there are two discrete outcomes
in another sense it is analog, the operation is continuous and the state is well-defined at all points during the operation
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that, by the traditional way of thinking, continuous-time quantum computing is somewhere between analog and digital, with a combination of properties that would not be allowed in a non-quantum setting.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Analog and Continuous-time Computers
quotes: By the traditional way of thinking, continuous-time quantum computing is somewhere between analog and digital
it has a combination of properties of both which would not be allowed in a non-quantum setting
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor educational page; no evidence offered beyond the text.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that for tasks in optimization and machine learning where conventional computing is limited, unconventional ways of thinking about computing are needed, and that quantum systems provide new ways to compute based on the continuous nature of quantum superpositions.
assertions.anchor: Lesson page, section Conclusion
quotes: For these tasks, such as those in optimization and machine learning, unconventional ways of thinking about computing are needed.
quantum systems provide new ways to compute, based on the continuous nature of quantum superpositions
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor states a conclusion that supports its own product line; the page gives no measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: The page shows no measured advantage of any unconventional system over a conventional one.

assertions.value: The page reports no experiment, benchmark, performance figure or citation to a named paper for any of its claims about QCi products. The authors point to a special issue and to a statement about analog tide predicting machines only as illustrations.
assertions.anchor: Whole page
quotes: The field is vast and contains many efforts where the goal is not so much to improve performance but to push the boundaries of our understanding of what a computer can be
assertions.certainty_reason: This is the reader's observation about the page as a whole, not a statement the page makes.
assertions.reader_inference: Reader observation: the lesson is educational vendor material and contains no data.
